--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Gears, Gear Trains, and Transmissions {#sec-chap-02-gears} ## Learning Objectives {#sec-objectives-04} By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: 1. **Explain** the fundamental principles of gear operation and power transmission 2. **Calculate** gear ratios, speed changes, and torque changes in gear systems 3. **Identify** different gear types and their appropriate applications 4. **Apply** gear terminology including module, diametral pitch, and pressure angle 5. **Analyze** simple, compound and planetary gear trains to determine overall speed ratios 6. **Design** a gear train that meets a speed, torque and size requirement ::: {.callout-think} **Before You Read:** Your car's engine might spin at 6,000 RPM, but your wheels only turn at about 1,000 RPM at highway speed. How does the transmission accomplish this speed reduction, and why is it necessary? ::: ## Introduction to Gears {#sec-gears-intro} Gears are toothed mechanical components that transmit **power and motion** between rotating shafts. They are among the oldest and most important machine elements, found in virtually every mechanical system—from wristwatches to wind turbines, from automotive transmissions to industrial robots. Gears serve four fundamental purposes: 1. **Transmit power** from one shaft to another 2. **Change rotational speed** (increase or decrease RPM) 3. **Change torque** (increase or decrease turning force) 4. **Change direction** of rotation or axis of rotation ## Fundamental Gear Concepts {#sec-gear-fundamentals} ### The Basic Principle When two gears mesh, their teeth interlock. As one gear (the **driver** or **pinion**) rotates, it pushes against the teeth of the other gear (the **driven gear**), causing it to rotate. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Basic gear mesh showing driver (pinion) and driven gear.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/gear-mesh-basic-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### The Fundamental Law of Gearing For smooth, constant-velocity power transmission, the **common normal** at the point of contact between gear teeth must always pass through a fixed point called the **pitch point**. This is achieved through the **involute tooth profile**, which is the standard for most modern gears. --- ## Gear Terminology {#sec-gear-terminology} Understanding gear terminology is essential for specifying, designing, and manufacturing gears. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Thread Standards](images/Gear-terminology-with-defination-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ### Essential Gear Formulas | Parameter | Metric (Module) | Imperial (Diametral Pitch) | |:----------|:----------------|:---------------------------| | **Pitch Diameter** | $d = m \times N$ | $d = N / P$ | | **Circular Pitch** | $p = \pi \times m$ | $p = \pi / P$ | | **Addendum** | $a = m$ | $a = 1 / P$ | | **Dedendum** | $b = 1.25 \times m$ | $b = 1.25 / P$ | | **Outside Diameter** | $d_o = m(N + 2)$ | $d_o = (N + 2) / P$ | | **Center Distance** | $C = m(N_1 + N_2)/2$ | $C = (N_1 + N_2) / 2P$ | Where: $m$ = module, $P$ = diametral pitch, $N$ = number of teeth, $d$ = pitch diameter > **⚠️ Important:** Module (mm) and Diametral Pitch (teeth/inch) are inversely related: $m = 25.4 / P$. **Never mix metric and imperial gears!** --- **Worked example: a 24-tooth pinion driving a 60-tooth gear, module 2 mm.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- 2 # module (mm) N1 <- 24 # pinion teeth N2 <- 60 # gear teeth d1 <- m * N1 # pitch diameters (mm) d2 <- m * N2 p <- pi * m # circular pitch (mm) do1 <- m * (N1 + 2) # outside diameters (mm) do2 <- m * (N2 + 2) C <- (d1 + d2) / 2 # centre distance (mm) cat("Pinion: d =", d1, "mm, outside diameter =", do1, "mm\n") cat("Gear: d =", d2, "mm, outside diameter =", do2, "mm\n") cat("Circular pitch p =", round(p, 2), "mm, addendum =", m, "mm, dedendum =", 1.25 * m, "mm\n") cat("Centre distance C =", C, "mm, gear ratio =", N2 / N1, ": 1\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pinion: d = 48 mm, outside diameter = 52 mm Gear: d = 120 mm, outside diameter = 124 mm Circular pitch p = 6.28 mm, addendum = 2 mm, dedendum = 2.5 mm Centre distance C = 84 mm, gear ratio = 2.5 : 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} *Live cell: change the module or either tooth count and watch the two gears resize. The pitch circles always touch at the pitch point.* ```{=html}

```
Show the worked solution **(a) Pitch Diameter:** $$d = m \times N = 3 \times 40 = 120 \text{ mm}$$ **(b) Outside Diameter:** $$d_o = m(N + 2) = 3(40 + 2) = 126 \text{ mm}$$ **(c) Circular Pitch:** $$p = \pi \times m = \pi \times 3 = 9.42 \text{ mm}$$
--- ## Types of Gears {#sec-gear-types} Different gear types are designed for different applications based on shaft orientation, load capacity, speed, and noise requirements. ### Spur Gears **Spur gears** have straight teeth parallel to the axis of rotation. They are the simplest, most common, and most economical type. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Spur Gear Animation](images/Animated_two_spur_gears_1_2.gif){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: **Advantages:** Simple, Economical, High efficiency (98-99%) **Disadvantages:** Noisy at high speeds, Limited to parallel shafts, Moderate load capacity **Applications:** Gearboxes, conveyors, food processing equipment, clocks, printers --- ### Helical Gears **Helical gears** have teeth cut at an angle (helix angle) to the shaft axis. This allows gradual tooth engagement, resulting in smoother, quieter operation. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Helical Gear Animation](images/Anim_engrenages_helicoidaux.gif){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: **Advantages:** Smoother, quieter, Higher load capacity, Can transmit power between non-parallel shafts **Disadvantages:** More complex to manufacture, Higher axial thrust, Slightly lower efficiency (97-99%) **Applications:** Automotive transmissions, industrial gearboxes, machine tools, elevators ### Herringbone Gears **Herringbone gears** are a special type of helical gear with two sets of teeth in a V-shaped pattern. This design cancels out axial thrust and allows for very high load capacity. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Herringbone Gear](images/Herringbone_gears_(Bentley,_Sketches_of_Engine_and_Machine_Details).jpg){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: **Advantages:** No axial thrust, Very high load capacity, Smooth operation **Disadvantages:** Complex and expensive to manufacture, Large size **Applications:** Heavy machinery, marine transmissions, power plants, large industrial gearboxes --- ### Bevel Gears **Bevel gears** transmit power between shafts that intersect, typically at 90°. The teeth are cut on a conical surface. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bevel Gear](images/Gear-kegelzahnrad.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: **Advantages:** Transmit power between intersecting shafts, Can achieve high reduction ratios, Smooth operation **Disadvantages:** More complex to design and manufacture, Higher cost, Moderate efficiency (97-99%) **Applications:** Automotive differentials, hand tools, food mixers, rotorcraft transmissions --- ### Worm Gears **Worm gears** consist of a worm (screw-like) driving a worm wheel. They provide very high reduction ratios in a compact space and can be self-locking. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Worm Gear](images/Worm_Gear.gif){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: **Advantages:** Very high reduction ratios, Compact design, Self-locking capability, Quiet operation **Disadvantages:** Low efficiency (40-90%), High sliding friction, More wear, Limited to right-angle shafts **Applications:** Conveyor drives, elevator lifts, tuning mechanisms, steering systems --- ### Rack and Pinion **Rack and pinion** converts rotational motion to linear motion (or vice versa). The rack is essentially a gear with infinite radius. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Rack and Pinion](images/Rack_and_pinion_animation.gif){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: **Advantages:** Simple, Precise linear motion, Can achieve high forces, Compact **Disadvantages:** Limited to linear applications, Moderate efficiency (97-99%), Wear on rack teeth **Applications:** Automotive steering, CNC machines, actuators, stairlifts --- ### Gear Type Comparison | Gear Type | Shaft Arrangement | Ratio Range | Efficiency | Noise Level | Cost | |:----------|:------------------|:------------|:-----------|:------------|:-----| | **Spur** | Parallel | 1:1 to 6:1 | 98-99% | High | Low | | **Helical** | Parallel | 1:1 to 10:1 | 97-99% | Low | Medium | | **Bevel** | Intersecting (90°) | 1:1 to 5:1 | 97-99% | Medium | High | | **Worm** | Right angle (non-intersecting) | 5:1 to 100:1 | 40-90% | Low | Medium | | **Rack & Pinion** | Rotary to linear | N/A | 97-99% | Medium | Medium | > **🤔 Design Decision:** A food packaging machine requires a 25:1 speed reduction in a compact space. The drive must be self-locking to prevent the load from back-driving the motor when power is off. Which gear type would you recommend?
Click to reveal analysis **Recommended: Worm Gear** Reasons: 1. **High ratio** - 25:1 is within the typical worm gear range (5:1 to 100:1) 2. **Compact** - Achieves high ratio in single stage 3. **Self-locking** - When lead angle < friction angle (typically < 5°), the worm gear cannot be back-driven 4. **Quiet operation** - Important in food processing environments **Trade-offs to consider:** - Lower efficiency (70-85% at this ratio) means more heat and energy loss - May require cooling or lubrication considerations - Higher sliding friction causes wear - use appropriate materials (bronze wheel, hardened steel worm)
--- ## Gear Ratios and Calculations {#sec-gear-ratios} ### Speed and Torque Relationships The **gear ratio** is the fundamental relationship between meshing gears: $$\text{Gear Ratio} = \frac{N_{driven}}{N_{driver}} = \frac{\omega_{driver}}{\omega_{driven}} = \frac{T_{driven}}{T_{driver}}$$ Where: $N$ = number of teeth, $\omega$ = angular velocity, $T$ = torque ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Gear ratio demonstration: speed reduction and torque multiplication.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/gear-ratio-visual-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### Key Relationships **For a simple gear pair:** | If the driven gear is... | Then speed is... | And torque is... | |:-------------------------|:-----------------|:-----------------| | **Larger** (more teeth) | **Reduced** | **Increased** | | **Smaller** (fewer teeth) | **Increased** | **Reduced** | | **Same size** | **Same** | **Same** | **Power relationship (accounting for efficiency):** $$P_{out} = P_{in} \times \eta$$ $$T_{out} \times \omega_{out} = T_{in} \times \omega_{in} \times \eta$$ Where $\eta$ = efficiency (typically 0.97-0.99 per gear mesh) --- A motor runs at 1750 RPM and delivers 5 kW. It drives a gear with 20 teeth meshed with a gear having 80 teeth. Calculate the gear ratio, the output speed, the input torque and the output torque (assume 98% efficiency). ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution **Gear ratio:** $$GR = \frac{N_{driven}}{N_{driver}} = \frac{80}{20} = 4:1$$ **Output speed:** $$n_{out} = \frac{n_{in}}{GR} = \frac{1750}{4} = 437.5 \text{ RPM}$$ **Input torque:** $$T_{in} = \frac{P}{\omega_{in}} = \frac{5000}{1750 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}} = \frac{5000}{183.3} = 27.3 \text{ N·m}$$ **Output torque:** $$T_{out} = T_{in} \times GR \times \eta = 27.3 \times 4 \times 0.98 = 107 \text{ N·m}$$ Or verify using power: $$T_{out} = \frac{P_{out}}{\omega_{out}} = \frac{5000 \times 0.98}{437.5 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}} = \frac{4900}{45.8} = 107 \text{ N·m}$$
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} *Live cell: change the tooth counts and the efficiency. Notice that power never changes, so every gain in torque is paid for in speed.* ```{=html}

```{webr-r} #| label: gear-pair-calc ## Edit these values and re-run! n_in <- 1750 ## motor speed (rpm) P_kW <- 5 ## input power (kW) N_driver <- 20 ## driver teeth N_driven <- 80 ## driven teeth eta_pct <- 98 ## mesh efficiency (%) GR <- N_driven / N_driver n_out <- n_in / GR T_in <- P_kW * 1000 / (n_in * 2 * pi / 60) T_out <- T_in * GR * eta_pct / 100 P_lost <- P_kW * 1000 * (1 - eta_pct / 100) ## Output torque against output speed for ratios from 1:1 to 20:1 (constant power) gr_seq <- seq(1, 20, by = 0.25) T_seq <- T_in * gr_seq * eta_pct / 100 par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) plot(n_in / gr_seq, T_seq, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "#2c3e50", xlab = "Output speed (rpm)", ylab = "Output torque (N m)", main = "Trading Speed for Torque") points(n_out, T_out, pch = 19, cex = 2.2, col = "#e74c3c") cat(sprintf("Output: %.1f rpm at %.0f N m\n", n_out, T_out)) cat(sprintf(" Gear ratio %.2f : 1\n", GR)) cat(sprintf(" Input torque %.1f N m\n", T_in)) cat(sprintf(" Output power %.0f W\n", P_kW * 1000 - P_lost)) cat(sprintf(" Lost as heat %.0f W\n", P_lost)) ```
::: --- ## Gear Trains {-} A **gear train** is a combination of two or more gears used to transmit power from one shaft to another. Gear trains allow for larger speed ratios and more complex motion transmission than a single gear pair. ### Simple Gear Train In a **simple gear train**, each shaft carries only one gear. The intermediate gears are called **idlers** and do not affect the overall gear ratio—they only change the direction of rotation. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simple gear train with idler gear.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/simple-gear-train-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: **Simple gear train ratio:** $$GR = \frac{N_{driven}}{N_{driver}} = \frac{N_{last}}{N_{first}}$$ The idler gears only affect **direction of rotation**, not the gear ratio. --- ### Compound Gear Train In a **compound gear train**, two or more gears are mounted on the same shaft, rotating together. This allows for much higher gear ratios in a compact space. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Compound gear train: higher ratios in less space.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/compound-gear-train-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: **Compound gear train ratio:** $$GR = \frac{N_{B}}{N_{A}} \times \frac{N_{D}}{N_{C}} = \frac{\text{Product of driven teeth}}{\text{Product of driver teeth}}$$ **Design it yourself.** The food-packaging drive in the case study later in this chapter needs 45 rpm (plus or minus 2%) from an 1800 rpm motor. A pinion with fewer than 17 teeth risks undercutting, and a gear larger than 120 teeth will not fit the housing. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} *Live cell: pick tooth counts for the two stages until the output speed lands in the window.* ```{=html}

```{webr-r} #| label: compound-train-calc ## Edit these values and re-run! n_in <- 1800 ## motor speed (rpm) N1 <- 18 ## stage 1 pinion teeth N2 <- 72 ## stage 1 gear teeth N3 <- 20 ## stage 2 pinion teeth N4 <- 60 ## stage 2 gear teeth m <- 3 ## module for both stages (mm) GR1 <- N2 / N1 GR2 <- N4 / N3 GR <- GR1 * GR2 n_mid <- n_in / GR1 n_out <- n_in / GR C1 <- m * (N1 + N2) / 2 ## centre distances (mm) C2 <- m * (N3 + N4) / 2 par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) bp <- barplot(c(n_in, n_mid, n_out), names.arg = c("Motor", "Middle shaft", "Output"), col = c("#2c3e50", "#7f8c8d", "#e67e22"), ylab = "Shaft speed (rpm)", main = "Speed Falls Stage by Stage") text(bp, c(n_in, n_mid, n_out), labels = round(c(n_in, n_mid, n_out), 1), pos = 3) if (n_out >= 44.1 && n_out <= 45.9) { cat(sprintf("Output speed: %.1f rpm - inside the 45 rpm +/- 2%% window\n", n_out)) } else { cat(sprintf("Output speed: %.1f rpm - !!outside the 45 rpm +/- 2%% window!!\n", n_out)) } cat(sprintf(" Stage 1 ratio %.2f : 1\n", GR1)) cat(sprintf(" Stage 2 ratio %.2f : 1\n", GR2)) cat(sprintf(" Overall ratio %.2f : 1\n", GR)) cat(sprintf(" Stage 1 centre distance %.1f mm\n", C1)) cat(sprintf(" Stage 2 centre distance %.1f mm\n", C2)) if (min(N1, N3) < 17) { cat(" Undercut check !!a pinion has fewer than 17 teeth!!\n") } else { cat(" Undercut check OK\n") } ```
::: --- ### Planetary (Epicyclic) Gear Train **Planetary gear systems** are compact, high-ratio gear trains widely used in automatic transmissions, power tools, and aerospace applications. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Planetary gear system components and arrangement.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/planetary-gear-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: **Planetary gear ratio** (sun input, carrier output, ring fixed): $$GR = 1 + \frac{N_{ring}}{N_{sun}}$$ **Applications:** - **Automotive:** Automatic transmissions, hybrid drives, transfer cases - **Aerospace:** Helicopter transmissions, jet engine gearboxes - **Industrial:** Wind turbines, conveyors, hoists ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} *Live cell: change the sun and ring tooth counts. The planet gears fill the gap, so the ring minus the sun must be an even number.* ```{=html}

Planetary Gear Set

```
Show the live R code behind this calculator

The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press Run Code to experiment further.

```{webr-r} #| label: planetary-calc ## Edit these values and re-run! n_sun <- 500 ## sun input speed (rpm) N_sun <- 30 ## sun gear teeth N_ring <- 60 ## ring gear teeth N_planet <- (N_ring - N_sun) / 2 ## planets must fill the gap between sun and ring GR_a <- 1 + N_ring / N_sun ## sun in, carrier out, ring fixed n_carrier <- n_sun / GR_a n_ring_rev <- -n_sun * N_sun / N_ring ## sun in, ring out, carrier fixed (reverse) n_sun_up <- n_sun * GR_a ## carrier in at n_sun, sun out, ring fixed par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) vals <- c(n_sun, n_carrier, n_ring_rev) bp <- barplot(vals, names.arg = c("Sun in", "Carrier out", "Ring out\n(carrier fixed)"), col = c("#2c3e50", "#e67e22", "#c0392b"), ylab = "Speed (rpm)", main = "Three Ways to Use One Gear Set") text(bp, vals, labels = round(vals, 1), pos = ifelse(vals >= 0, 3, 1)) cat(sprintf("Carrier speed: %.1f rpm (ratio %.2f : 1)\n", n_carrier, GR_a)) if (N_planet == round(N_planet)) { cat(sprintf(" Planet gear teeth %d\n", N_planet)) } else { cat(" Planet gear teeth !!not a whole number: ring minus sun must be even!!\n") } cat(sprintf(" Ring out, carrier fixed %.1f rpm (reversed)\n", n_ring_rev)) cat(sprintf(" Carrier in at %g rpm, sun out %.1f rpm (speed increase)\n", n_sun, n_sun_up)) ```
::: > **🤔 Automotive Connection:** Why do automatic transmissions use planetary gear sets instead of conventional gear trains?
Click to reveal explanation **Planetary gears in automatic transmissions offer several advantages:** 1. **Multiple ratios from one gear set** - By holding different elements (sun, ring, or carrier) stationary using clutches and bands, different gear ratios are achieved without physically moving gears 2. **Constant mesh** - All gears remain engaged; ratio changes are smooth and fast 3. **Compact design** - High power density; fits in limited space 4. **Load sharing** - Multiple planet gears share the load (typically 3-5 planets) 5. **Coaxial input/output** - Input and output shafts can be on the same axis A typical 6-speed automatic uses 2-3 planetary gear sets with multiple clutches to achieve all forward gears plus reverse.
**From gear ratio to engine speed.** A vehicle's road speed ties the engine, the transmission, the final drive and the tyre together: $$n_{engine} = \frac{v}{2\pi r_{tyre}} \times 60 \times i_{gear} \times i_{final}$$ where $v$ is in m/s, $r_{tyre}$ in m and $i$ are the ratios of the selected gear and the final drive. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} *Live cell: find the overdrive ratio that keeps the engine relaxed at motorway speed.* ```{=html}

Show the live R code behind this calculator

The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press Run Code to experiment further.

```{webr-r} #| label: vehicle-cruise-calc ## Edit these values and re-run! road_speed <- 120 ## road speed (km/h) gear_ratio <- 1 ## transmission ratio of the selected gear final_drive <- 3.73 ## final drive (differential) ratio tire_r <- 0.34 ## tyre rolling radius (m) v_ms <- road_speed / 3.6 wheel_rpm <- v_ms / (2 * pi * tire_r) * 60 engine_rpm <- wheel_rpm * gear_ratio * final_drive ## Engine speed against road speed for the chosen ratios v_seq <- seq(40, 200, by = 5) rpm_seq <- v_seq / 3.6 / (2 * pi * tire_r) * 60 * gear_ratio * final_drive par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) plot(v_seq, rpm_seq, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "#2c3e50", xlab = "Road speed (km/h)", ylab = "Engine speed (rpm)", main = "Engine Speed vs. Road Speed") abline(h = 2600, lty = 2, col = "#bdc3c7") points(road_speed, engine_rpm, pch = 19, cex = 2.2, col = "#e74c3c") fmt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE) if (engine_rpm <= 2600) { cat(sprintf("Engine speed: %s rpm - relaxed cruise\n", fmt(engine_rpm))) } else { cat(sprintf("Engine speed: %s rpm - !!above the 2600 rpm cruise target!!\n", fmt(engine_rpm))) } cat(sprintf(" Wheel speed %s rpm\n", fmt(wheel_rpm))) cat(sprintf(" Overall ratio, engine/wheel %.2f : 1\n", gear_ratio * final_drive)) ```
::: --- ## Industry Applications {-} ### Automotive Industry ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Gear applications in automotive systems.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/automotive-gears-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: **Key automotive gear applications:** | System | Gear Types | Purpose | |:-------|:-----------|:--------| | Manual Transmission | Helical, synchronizer | Multiple speed ratios | | Automatic Transmission | Planetary, helical | Smooth ratio changes | | Differential | Spiral bevel, hypoid | Final drive, allows wheel speed difference | | Transfer Case | Spur, chain/gear | 4WD/AWD power distribution | | Steering | Rack and pinion, recirculating ball | Convert rotation to linear | | Starter Motor | Spur, planetary | High reduction for cranking torque | --- ### Food Processing Industry ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Gear applications in food processing equipment: a worm-gear conveyor drive, a planetary mixer head and a gear-driven packaging indexer.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/food-industry-gears-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: **Food industry gear requirements:** - **Stainless steel** or **food-grade materials** for hygiene - **Sealed gearboxes** to prevent lubricant contamination - **Washdown capability** for sanitation - **Smooth operation** to prevent product damage - **Variable speed** capability for different products --- ### Defense Industry ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Gear applications in defense systems: a vehicle drivetrain, a gear-driven turret ring and a harmonic drive actuator.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/defense-gears-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: **Defense gear requirements:** - **Extreme reliability** - Mission critical, no field repair - **High strength-to-weight ratio** - Often use aerospace-grade materials - **Environmental resistance** - Temperature extremes, dust, water - **Zero or minimal backlash** - Precision positioning systems - **Noise reduction** - Stealth requirements - **Shock loading capability** - Combat conditions --- ## Gear Design Considerations {#sec-gear-design} ### Material Selection | Material | Applications | Advantages | Limitations | |:---------|:-------------|:-----------|:------------| | **Carbon Steel** (1045, 4140) | General purpose, automotive | Good strength, economical | Requires heat treatment | | **Alloy Steel** (4340, 8620) | High-load applications | High strength, hardenable | More expensive | | **Cast Iron** | Low-speed, low-load | Good damping, economical | Brittle, low strength | | **Bronze** | Worm wheels, low-speed | Good wear with steel | Lower strength | | **Nylon/Acetal** | Light loads, quiet operation | Self-lubricating, quiet | Limited load, temperature | | **Stainless Steel** | Food, medical, marine | Corrosion resistant | Lower hardness possible | ### Common Failure Modes ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Common gear failure modes.](02-02-Gears_files/figure-html/gear-failures-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ### Design Guidelines 1. **Minimum teeth:** To avoid undercut (20° pressure angle): - Minimum pinion teeth ≈ 17 for standard gears - Use profile shift for fewer teeth 2. **Contact ratio:** Should be > 1.2 for smooth operation $$\text{Contact Ratio} = \frac{\text{Arc of Action}}{\text{Circular Pitch}}$$ 3. **Face width:** Typically 9-13 × module for spur gears 4. **Backlash:** Small clearance between teeth (typically 0.04-0.10 × module) 5. **Lubrication:** Critical for all enclosed gear systems --- ## Design Checklist for Gears {-} ### Gear Specification - [ ] Gear type selected based on shaft arrangement - [ ] Module/diametral pitch specified - [ ] Number of teeth determined for required ratio - [ ] Pressure angle specified (typically 20°) - [ ] Face width determined - [ ] Material selected based on load and environment ### Strength Verification - [ ] Bending stress calculated and within limits - [ ] Contact (Hertzian) stress calculated and within limits - [ ] Service factors applied for shock loading - [ ] Safety factor adequate (typically 1.5-2.5) ### Gear Train Design - [ ] Overall ratio achieved - [ ] Intermediate shafts and bearings specified - [ ] Center distances calculated - [ ] Shaft alignment considered - [ ] Housing/mounting provisions adequate ### Manufacturing and Assembly - [ ] Gear quality grade specified (AGMA or ISO) - [ ] Surface finish requirements defined - [ ] Heat treatment specified if required - [ ] Assembly procedure considered - [ ] Lubrication system designed --- ## Case Study: Food Packaging Line Drive {-} **Design Requirements:** A food packaging machine requires a gear drive with the following specifications: * Motor speed: 1800 RPM * Output speed: 45 RPM (±2%) * Output torque: 200 N·m * Must fit in 300 mm × 200 mm envelope * Food-safe requirements (no contamination risk) * 16 hours/day operation, 6 days/week > **🤔 Your Turn:** Design a gear train to meet these requirements. Consider gear types, stages, materials, and food safety.
Click to reveal design solution **1. Calculate Required Ratio:** $$GR = \frac{1800}{45} = 40:1$$ **2. Select Gear Train Configuration:** **Option A: Two-stage helical** (preferred for food industry) - Stage 1: 6.3:1 (16T pinion, 101T gear - round to 100T) → actual 6.25:1 - Stage 2: 6.4:1 (15T pinion, 96T gear) → actual 6.4:1 - Total: 6.25 × 6.4 = **40:1** ✓ **Option B: Worm + Helical** - Worm stage: 20:1 - Helical stage: 2:1 - Total: 40:1 - Self-locking feature may be beneficial **3. Material Selection:** - Gears: **Stainless steel 17-4 PH** (food-safe, hardenable) - Alternative: Carbon steel with **food-grade coating** - Housing: Cast aluminum with epoxy coating **4. Food Safety Features:** - **Sealed gearbox** with NSF-approved seals - **Food-grade synthetic lubricant** (NSF H1) - **Smooth exterior** for easy cleaning - **Stainless fasteners** **5. Verify Size:** - Module 3 for both stages - Stage 1 center distance: 3 × (16 + 100) / 2 = 174 mm - Stage 2 center distance: 3 × (15 + 96) / 2 = 166.5 mm - Fits within 300 × 200 mm envelope ✓ **6. Efficiency Check:** - Two-stage helical: ~97% × 97% = 94% - Input power: (200 × 45 × 2π/60) / 0.94 = 1003 W - Motor rating: 1.1 kW minimum ✓

Gear A (18 teeth) on shaft 1 drives gear B (54 teeth); gear C (20 teeth) is on the same shaft as B and drives gear D (60 teeth) on shaft 3. Shaft 3 is the sun gear input of a planetary stage with $N_{sun} = 24$ and $N_{ring} = 72$, with the ring fixed and the carrier as output. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution $$n_2 = 1500 \times \frac{18}{54} = 500 \text{ rpm}, \qquad n_3 = 500 \times \frac{20}{60} = 166.7 \text{ rpm}$$ $$GR_{planetary} = 1 + \frac{72}{24} = 4, \qquad n_{out} = \frac{166.7}{4} = 41.67 \text{ rpm}, \qquad GR_{total} = 36:1$$ The overall ratio is the product of the stage ratios: $3 \times 3 \times 4 = 36$.

### Try it yourself: which gear type? {#sec-tryit-gear-types} ```{=html}
``` ## Key Takeaways {#sec-gear-takeaways} - The gear ratio is driven teeth over driver teeth. It divides speed and multiplies torque, and power stays constant apart from the mesh losses. - Module and diametral pitch are inverse measures of tooth size, and meshing gears must share the same one. - Idlers change direction, not ratio. Compound trains multiply stage ratios in a compact space. - A planetary set with the ring fixed, sun input and carrier output gives $1 + N_{ring}/N_{sun}$. - Pick the gear type from the shaft arrangement, speed, noise and whether the drive must self-lock. ## Practice Problems {#sec-gear-problems} **Problem 1:** A spur gear has 24 teeth and a module of 4 mm. Calculate the pitch diameter, circular pitch, addendum and outside diameter. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution **(a) Pitch Diameter:** $$d = m \times N = 4 \times 24 = 96 \text{ mm}$$ **(b) Circular Pitch:** $$p = \pi \times m = \pi \times 4 = 12.57 \text{ mm}$$ **(c) Addendum:** $$a = m = 4 \text{ mm}$$ **(d) Outside Diameter:** $$d_o = m(N + 2) = 4(24 + 2) = 104 \text{ mm}$$
--- **Problem 2:** A compound gear train has: Gear A (20 teeth) driving Gear B (50 teeth), which is on the same shaft as Gear C (18 teeth), which drives Gear D (72 teeth). Calculate the overall gear ratio and output speed if the input is 1200 RPM. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution **Gear Ratio:** $$GR = \frac{N_B}{N_A} \times \frac{N_D}{N_C} = \frac{50}{20} \times \frac{72}{18} = 2.5 \times 4 = 10:1$$ **Output Speed:** $$n_{out} = \frac{n_{in}}{GR} = \frac{1200}{10} = 120 \text{ RPM}$$
--- **Problem 3:** A planetary gear set has a sun gear with 20 teeth and a ring gear with 80 teeth. If the ring is held stationary and the sun is the input at 500 RPM, what is the carrier (output) speed? ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution For sun input, carrier output, ring fixed: $$GR = 1 + \frac{N_{ring}}{N_{sun}} = 1 + \frac{80}{20} = 1 + 4 = 5:1$$ **Carrier Speed:** $$n_{carrier} = \frac{n_{sun}}{GR} = \frac{500}{5} = 100 \text{ RPM}$$
